name: Word classes and sentence structure
intro: The main word classes in English, basic word order, and how knowing them helps you write clearer and more correct sentences.
sammendrag:
## Why grammar?

Knowing the **word classes** (parts of speech) and how English sentences are built helps you understand texts, avoid common mistakes and explain why something is right or wrong. Many terms are similar to Norwegian grammar, which makes them easier to learn.

## The main word classes

- **Nouns** name people, places, things and ideas: teacher, London, happiness. Most nouns have a plural form: book – books, child – children.
- **Verbs** show actions or states: run, think, be. Verbs change with tense: walk – walked.
- **Adjectives** describe nouns: a **tall** building, the book is **boring**. English adjectives do not change for plural: tall buildings.
- **Adverbs** describe verbs, adjectives or whole sentences, often telling how, when or where: She sings **beautifully**. Many adverbs end in **-ly**.
- **Pronouns** replace nouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they, me, him, her, us, them.
- **Prepositions** show relations in place and time: in, on, at, under, after.
- **Conjunctions** join words and clauses: and, but, or, because, although.
- **Determiners** come before nouns: a, an, the, this, my, some.

## Articles

Use **a** before a consonant sound and **an** before a vowel sound: a book, an apple, **an hour** (silent h), **a university** (the word starts with a “you” sound). **The** is used about something specific or already mentioned.

## Word order

The basic word order in an English statement is **subject – verb – object** (S-V-O): **Emma** (S) **likes** (V) **pizza** (O). Unlike Norwegian, English keeps this order even when a sentence starts with a time expression: “Yesterday **I went** to the cinema”, not “Yesterday went I”.

Questions and negatives with most verbs need the helping verb **do/does/did**: Do you like pizza? She does not (doesn't) like fish.

## Sentences and clauses

A **sentence** starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. A **clause** contains a subject and a verb. A **main clause** can stand alone: I stayed at home. A **subordinate clause** cannot: because it was raining. Together they form a **complex sentence**: I stayed at home because it was raining.

## Using grammar when you write

When you revise your own texts, check that every sentence has a subject and a verb, that word order is S-V-O, that you have used a/an correctly, and that you have not written a subordinate clause on its own as a full sentence.

flashcards.def: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea: teacher, Oslo, happiness.
A word that shows an action or a state: run, think, be.
A word that describes a noun: a tall building. Does not change in the plural.
Describes a verb, adjective or sentence, often how, when or where. Many end in -ly.
A word that replaces a noun: I, you, she, they, them.
Shows relation in place or time: in, on, at, under, after.
Joins words and clauses: and, but, or, because.
Comes before a noun: a, the, this, my, some.
“a” before a consonant sound, “an” before a vowel sound: an hour, a university.
Subject – verb – object: basic English word order. Emma likes pizza.
English keeps S-V: “Yesterday I went”, not “Yesterday went I”.
Questions and negatives with most verbs use do/does/did: Do you like it?
A group of words with a subject and a verb.
A clause that can stand alone as a sentence.
A clause that cannot stand alone: because it was raining.

quiz.text: Which word is an adjective in “The old dog slept quietly”?
quiz.explain: “Old” describes the noun “dog”. “Quietly” is an adverb describing how the dog slept.
“Hour” starts with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so we use “an”.

quiz.text: Which sentence has correct English word order?
options: Yesterday I went to the cinema.
Yesterday I to the cinema went.
Yesterday I went the cinema to.
Yesterday went to the cinema I.
quiz.explain: English keeps subject + verb even when the sentence starts with a time expression.
“Because” joins a subordinate clause to a main clause.

quiz.text: How do you make “She likes fish” negative?
quiz.explain: Most verbs need do-support in negatives. With he/she/it we use “does not” (doesn't) + the base form.

quiz.text: What is the subject in “My brother plays football”?
quiz.explain: The subject is who does the action: my brother.

quiz.text: Which is NOT a complete sentence?
quiz.explain: “Because it was raining” is a subordinate clause and cannot stand alone.
“Beautifully” tells how something is done. Many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective.
English adjectives never take a plural ending. Only the noun changes: buildings.

ekstra.text: English adjectives get an -s in the plural, like “bigs cars”.
ekstra.explain: English adjectives never change for plural: big cars.

ekstra.text: “An” is used before words that start with a vowel sound.
ekstra.explain: It is the sound, not the letter, that decides: an hour, a university.

ekstra.text: A subordinate clause can stand alone as a full sentence.
ekstra.explain: A subordinate clause needs a main clause to make a complete sentence.
“Under” shows a relation in place: under the table.
Questions with most verbs need “do” before the subject: Do you like pizza?
“Them” replaces a noun, for example “the students”.

ekstra.text: Which article is correct? “She is … engineer.”
ekstra.explain: “Engineer” starts with a vowel sound, so we use “an”. English also needs an article with jobs: She is an engineer.

skriv.text: Explain the difference between a noun and a pronoun. Give an example where a pronoun replaces a noun, such as “teacher” being replaced by “she”.
skriv.fasit: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. A pronoun replaces a noun: “The teacher is here. She is here.”
kriterier: Explains that a noun names a person, place, thing or idea.
Explains that a pronoun replaces a noun, with an example that shows this.

skriv.text: Change “a tall building” to the plural. Explain what happens to the adjective.
skriv.fasit: The plural is “tall buildings”. The adjective “tall” does not change in the plural.
kriterier: Gives “tall buildings” as the plural form.
Explains that the adjective stays the same in the plural.

skriv.text: Explain why both “an hour” and “a university” use the correct article.
skriv.fasit: “An” comes before a vowel sound, and the h in “hour” is silent. “University” starts with a “you” sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes “a”.
kriterier: Connects “an” in “an hour” to the vowel sound at the start.
Connects “a” in “a university” to its starting consonant sound.

skriv.text: Why is “Yesterday I went to the cinema” correct, while “Yesterday went I to the cinema” is not?
skriv.fasit: Even when a time expression comes first, English keeps the subject before the verb. In the correct sentence, “I” comes before “went”.
kriterier: Explains that the subject stays before the verb after a time expression.
Uses the sentence to show that “I” must come before “went”.

skriv.text: Turn “You like music.” into a question. Explain the job of the extra verb you add.
skriv.fasit: “Do you like music?” The helping verb “do” is used to form the question.
kriterier: Forms the question as “Do you like music?” or an equivalent correct question.
Explains that “do” is a helping verb used to form the question.

skriv.text: Why can “because it was raining” not stand alone as a sentence? Add a main clause to make it a complex sentence.
skriv.fasit: It has a subject and a verb, but it is a subordinate clause and cannot stand alone. “I stayed at home because it was raining” is a complex sentence.
kriterier: Explains that the clause is subordinate and cannot stand alone.
Adds a main clause that can stand alone and forms a complex sentence with the given clause.

skriv.text: Compare the adjective in “a quiet room” with the adverb in “speaks quietly”. What does each word describe?
skriv.fasit: “Quiet” is an adjective that describes the noun “room”. “Quietly” is an adverb that describes the verb “speaks”.
kriterier: Explains that the adjective describes a noun.
Explains that the adverb describes a verb.

skriv.text: Write one English sentence that contains a preposition showing place or time and a conjunction joining clauses. Name both words and explain what each one does.
skriv.fasit: “The book is on the desk because I need it.” “On” is a preposition showing place, and “because” is a conjunction joining clauses.
kriterier: Uses a preposition correctly to show a relation in place or time.
Uses a conjunction to join words or clauses and explains its role.
